explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on the “first word” of little boilerplate or header lines across genres—e.g. the SPDX tag in C++ comments (SPD), the weekday in an email Date (Wed), the legal‐citation term in court notices (estoppel), UI prompts (Please, Enter), judge‐panel labels (Before), or hedging in license disclaimers (hope). It flags tokens that kick off structured metadata or section headings in text.
This feature is a detector for the sentence-final period (the full stop) in formal scientific/technical prose, i.e. it lights up on the “.” that marks the end of a sentence in research-style writing.

This feature isn’t picking out any particular meaning like “tiger” or “tundra,” but rather is a purely orthographic/subword detector: it fires on tokens that contain short “u-centered” n-grams (qu, ut, ug, und, tig, lig, etc.). In other words, it’s a character-level pattern detector for sequences with “u” plus one or more consonants (and the special “qu” bigram) that recur across many languages and contexts.
This neuron fires on the sentence-final period (full stop) token, i.e. the “.” that marks the end of a sentence.

This neuron is basically an n-gram detector for the little “om/ro/-om-” letter pattern that turns up as a Greek/Latin root or acronym piece in lots of technical vocab (e.g. Zometa, POM, nanocomposites, pheochromocytoma, progestagens, pyrocarbonate, Schroeder, Saprolegnia, SubCategory, multiplier). It flags that short substring wherever it appears across domains.

This neuron is basically an “adjectival‐modifier” detector.  It spikes on descriptive tokens—especially past‐participle/“-ed” forms (reformed, harassed, disabled, updated, died, retarded, defective), plus other adjective endings (-ous, ‑ive, ‑ic, etc., e.g. continuous, durable, invalid, pathogenic)—typically in title‐ or heading-style contexts (often right before a closing punctuation).

explanations.explanation: This neuron is simply firing whenever the model sees a very short subword token – one to three characters long (often including a diacritic or non-Latin character) – that typically functions as a little “piece” or affix inside a word or name.  In other words, it’s a detector for tiny BPE chunks (like “ä”, “γ”, “و” or “Fa,” “Ev,” “ab,” “inc,” “cc,” “ef,” etc.) that recur across languages and scripts as standalone subword units.
This neuron fires on the central “object” word in a technical how-to or troubleshooting question—i.e. the key resource or thing being manipulated (tunnel, path, string, mount, pins, etc.).

This feature fires on classical (mostly Greek/Latin) scientific morphemes—especially color- or chemistry-derived roots like xanth-, anthr-, porph-, pyrethr-, etc.—marking key pieces of chemical names, pigment terms and taxonomic labels in bioscience texts.
The feature flags the key “topic” noun in titles or opening noun‐phrases—the primary subject or entity introduced at the start of a section (e.g. “offices,” “screens,” “teams,” “Jenkins,” etc.).

explanations.explanation: This feature is sensitive to structural “label” tokens in technical or semi-structured text—things like identifiers serving as keys or headings (e.g. JSON/XML/code field names immediately followed by “:”), the second element of formal multi-word labels (e.g. STATES in “UNITED STATES COURT”), and even the corner/edge symbols in ASCII-art box diagrams.

This feature lights up on the initial, capitalized “prefix” in multi-word names or titles—especially in Camel/PascalCase identifiers and product-style headings (e.g. “Quick” in QuickStart, QuickBooks or “Down” in DownTimeNotification, DownCircledOutlined). It abstracts the role of the leading descriptor in compound brand, component, or guide names.

This feature lights up on English words that denote actions, processes or fields—mostly gerunds/participles and related nominalizations formed with suffixes like ­-ing, ­-ation/­-ization, ­-ure/­-ivated, etc.—the kinds of nouns or adjectives you see in titles, headings, and activity-oriented terms (e.g. “cultivated,” “playing,” “flying,” “foraging,” “mobilization,” “boosting,” “agriculture”).

The feature is a “begin-of-entity/title word” detector – it fires on the initial subword of capitalized, content-bearing tokens (proper names, organizations, species names, headline terms) across diverse text.

The feature is picking out small fixed letter‐n-grams—especially consonant clusters and two-letter acronyms (e.g. “wr,” “sh,” “osh,” “rw,” “DW,” “Wh,” “DQ”)—regardless of whether they occur in ordinary words (wrinkles, photoshoot, shuffle) or technical identifiers and codes (pthread_rwlock, Diffusion-Weighted “DW,” kWh, base-64 “DQ”).

This neuron is a “named-entity/abbreviation” detector in formal prose.  It spikes on the key tokens that anchor people, organizations, dates, titles and other standardized labels—proper first names (Connie, Brian, Marcus), role-titles (Gov., Chief, founding member, Capital Planning), group headers (Members, Citizens), corporate and degree suffixes (Corp., M.Ed.), date and part abbreviations (Sept., Oct., Part 2.), even technical section markers (component)—all the bits that signal the start or core of an entity or headed section rather than ordinary running text.

This head is detecting subword trigrams of the form “M-vowel-liquid/nasal” (e.g. mal-, mar-, mon-, lum-, mamm-), so it fires on Latin/Greek roots and proper names built on that pattern (“malignant,” “Lamar,” “lumina,” “mammary,” “Marsh,” “monitor,” “jambalaya,” etc.).
This neuron fires on short, all‐caps letter clusters—i.e. acronyms, initialisms or model/name abbreviations (e.g. “PRO,” “RT,” “TR,” “RTV,” etc.) across varied domains.

This neuron is a “number/measurement” detector—it lights up on isolated numeric (or short alphanumeric) tokens that convey key quantitative parameters (ages, sizes, pH values, bit-widths, nanometer process nodes, decimal fractions, data rates, etc.) across technical and scientific contexts.

This feature detects the word “Blog” (and close variants) when it’s used as a UI label or metadata tag in web‐page contexts—e.g. headings, archive/category labels or navigation elements that mark content as a blog post.

This neuron is essentially a “capital-G” bigram/cluster detector.  It lights up on tokens that start with or prominently feature “G” (often followed by another letter like r, j, o or doubled g), so it flags government abbreviations (Gov), reference-marker fragments (r in “ref”), proper names (Wiggins, Morris), academic or language-specific digraphs (Grads, progrès, gjennomgangen), etc.  In short, it detects tokens whose salient orthography begins with G-sequences common in names, acronyms, and labels.

This neuron fires whenever the model sees the start of a named‐entity or technical term token—proper names, place/organization labels, acronyms or domain-specific labels (e.g. “Dalatyr,” “Dalai,” “NAACP,” “LaPort,” “alanine,” “Eleazar,” etc.).

This neuron is a sub‐word “liquid+vowel” detector—i.e. it strongly fires on token chunks that start with an English liquid consonant (r or l) plus a vowel (ri, ro, rou, lu, gri, ou, etc.), a pattern that crops up at the beginnings of many roots, names, and technical terms.

This neuron fires on tokens that serve as formal labels or headings in titles—that is, capitalized category words (Month, Season, Process, Execution, September) and short all‐caps acronyms (PH, DM, SEM, HSP, CM) used to name events, methods or technical domains.

This feature detects the notion of quantitative aggregation or enumeration—tokens that denote counting or ranking (e.g. “Count/​counts” in code and prose, SQL COUNT, .Count properties, thread-count, eosinophil counts, search “Rank,” etc.).

Here’s a concise interpretation for each high-activation subword feature:

• Vine  
  Recognizes “Vine” as a proper‐name component in project or company titles (e.g. Project Vine, Vineyard Wind).

• Su  
  Flags the “su” prefix in specialized terms: clinical/psychiatric (“suicidal…”) and technical/math notation (Δ^su+…).

• Eva  
  Marks the female given name “Eva” when used as a proper noun across profiles and narratives.

• soy  
  Identifies “soy” in scientific/food‐science contexts relating to soybean systems, proteins and isoflavones.

• veter  
  Captures the veterinary stem in words about animal‐health professionals (veterinarians, veterinary).

• Edu  
  Highlights the “Edu” prefix in branding of educational or simulation platforms (EducaSimula, etc.).

• EV  
  Detects the “EVR”/“EV” acronym in programming contexts, specifically Microsoft’s Enhanced Video Renderer API.

• Ven  
  Picks out “Ven” in product‐brand names, notably cannabis extracts (e.g. Venom OG Concentrate).

• vie  
  Spots the verb “vie” meaning “compete,” especially in idioms like “vie for supremacy.”

• Veg  
  Flags the “Veg” prefix in vegan/vegetarian food and lifestyle branding (e.g. Vegan-Ease).

This feature fires on tokens that serve as high-level categorical labels or names—typically uppercase or CamelCase markers that tag entities (e.g. journal abbreviations like “J GRA,” Roman-numeral study phases “II,” organization or political titles like “Revolutionary” or “National,” and software/class/plugin identifiers such as “DynamicImport,” “MathJax,” “JTextField”).

This feature is essentially a “spo-” substring detector—it fires on subword tokens beginning with the sequence spo- (or variants like spi-/spe-) as in spoil, spoiler, spoilage, spoils, spoiling, etc., regardless of the surrounding topic.

This feature flags the leading descriptive word in multi‐word category or proper‐name phrases—i.e. the first modifier that defines a place, time period, demographic group, UI section, etc. Examples: “Lower” (Manhattan, Silesia, Snake River, Broadway, Carniola), “Early”/“Late” (childhood, subtypes), “Elderly,” “Home” (menu or homecoming), and other initial labels in titles and names.

This neuron is a “v‐detector”: it strongly activates on subword tokens containing the letter “v” (especially at the start of the piece, e.g. “av” in Pavela/Paviot/Pavakka, “Nav” in Navarro/Navigation, “IPV”, “PPV”, “inv” in invisible, etc.), regardless of whether they’re names, acronyms, or common words.

This feature detects morphological modifiers—adverbial intensifiers and derivational prefixes/adjectives (e.g. “fully,” “semi-,” “poly-,” “phospho-,” “compulsory,” “structurally,” “follicular,” “cylindrical,” “parental”)—that occur in formal scientific and technical prose to specify properties or degrees.
This neuron fires on the leading piece of a Title-Case or all-caps token – i.e. the initial subword of a capitalized word (proper names, headings, class or section titles, acronyms).

This feature is a “root‐spotter” for Latin/Greek stems in formal/scientific vocabulary—e.g. calor-, reduct-, protec-, calc-, compens-, contract-, duct-, degrad-, fund-, cortic-, etc.—marking the core morpheme of complex technical terms.

explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on small integer tokens (whether written as digits or words) when they’re used as dates, counts or simple enumerations in formal text.

This feature fires on attributive adjectives or adjectival stems (often –ic/–al/–ive endings) that classify or qualify a noun by domain, subtype or locale—e.g. organ-specific (pancreatic, gastric, intervertebral), geographic or cultural (Catalan, Western, Eastern, Pacific), organizational or technical (Cloud, global), or property descriptors (conservative, peripheral).

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on abstract common nouns in the plural—“things” or conceptual items (decisions, values, notions, answers, analogues, factors, choices, changes, terms, expectations, etc.) that are the focal objects or endpoints under discussion.
This feature detects the full-stop that terminates an abbreviation—most often the period after a single-letter initial (as in middle initials, legal citation abbrevs or acronyms, and similar forms).

A concise way to describe this feature is:
It flags adjectival stems and bound affixes used as compound modifiers in technical text (e.g. initial-, direct, dose-dependent, site-specific, long-term, anti-, pro-, post-) that qualify nouns or variables.
